prime.problem: You now hold a 27×27 tensor of 228,146 counts. Printed raw, it is 729 unlabelled integers, so you can't see what the model has learned or spot the cells that will cause trouble later.
prime.fits: It follows the counting card, where N[ix1, ix2] += 1 built the table. Here you learn to read it: which axis is which, what a row means, and why a single '.' token beats <S>/<E>. The next card turns one row into probabilities and samples from it.
expect: row = current character, column = next character
prime.goal: Look up any pair in N, read a row as "what comes next", and explain why the 27×27 layout with '.' wastes nothing that the 28×28 one did.

attend: Why does each row of N, and not each column, answer the question the model needs at sampling time?
Why do pairs that touch '.' dominate the top of the ranking, even though '.' never appears inside a name?
What exactly did merging <S> and <E> into one '.' remove from the table?
Why must the 'e' row total equal the 'e' column total, and what does the '.' row total count?
What can the heatmap's colour not tell you about a cell, and where will that gap matter?

must: Counting uses N[stoi[ch1], stoi[ch2]] → the row is the current character and the column is the next one → one row holds everything the data says about "what follows this letter" → dividing a row by its total gives the next-character distribution the model samples from
Every name has exactly one start and one end → the '.' row and '.' column each collect 32,033 counts spread over only 26 letters → boundary pairs like n. (6,763) and a. (6,640) top the whole table

<E> is never followed by anything and <S> never follows anything → in the 28×28 layout a whole row and column are always zero (55 cells) → one '.' token plays both roles → 27×27 with only N[0,0] structurally zero

The colour scale is linear up to 6,763 → a count of 14 looks as blank as 0 → you can't see impossible pairs by eye → check (N == 0).sum() (102), because a zero count later becomes a probability of 0 and an infinite loss
elevated: Each character is counted once as the first of a pair and once as the second → row total = column total = how often it appears (20,423 for 'e'; 32,033 names for '.') → a quick sanity check that your counting loop is right
reference: .item() to turn a one-element tensor into a Python int

compress.prompt: From memory, sketch a 4×4 corner of N (rows and columns . a e n), mark which axis is "current" and which is "next", and write 3–4 sentences on how to read a row, what the '.' row and column hold, and why the '.' token replaced <S>/<E>.
checklist: row = current character, column = next character; a cell counts that pair
a row read left to right is the next-character distribution (before normalising)
row 0 = first letters, column 0 = last letters, and each sums to the 32,033 names
<S>/<E> left a whole row and column empty; one '.' removes that waste
pale does not mean zero: rare and impossible pairs look alike on the picture

retrieve.q: Explain why the most common cells in N are boundary pairs (n., a., .a) rather than pairs inside names.
answer: each name contributes exactly one start pair and one end pair
those 32,033 counts land in only 26 cells each (row 0, column 0)
pairs inside names are spread over hundreds of cells, so each gets a smaller share

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens to N when the loop processes the name "emma": which five cells change, and by how much?
answer: the name becomes . e m m a ., giving pairs .e, em, mm, ma, a.
each pair adds 1 at row stoi[first], column stoi[second]
the '.' row and '.' column totals each go up by one (one name)

retrieve.q: You want to know which pairs never occur. Compare looking at the imshow picture with computing (N == 0). What does each give you and where does each fail?
answer: the picture shows structure at a glance (dark rows, the empty top-left cell)
its linear colour scale makes counts like 14 or 1 indistinguishable from 0
(N == 0) is exact (102 cells) but gives no overview
use the picture to explore and code to check

retrieve.q: The 'a' row totals 33,885 and the 'q' row only 272. Why is comparing the darkness of cells across these two rows misleading, and what fixes it?
answer: raw counts mix how common the first letter is with how predictable the next one is
a lighter cell in a rare row can be a larger share of that row
divide each row by its own total to get probabilities, then compare

compare.q: The dict of pair counts and the 27×27 tensor hold the same 228,146 counts. What does the grid layout make easy that the dict does not, and what does it cost?
answer: the grid puts all of a letter's successors in one row, ready to normalise and sample
it also makes zeros explicit: every one of the 729 possible pairs has a cell
the dict stores only pairs that occurred (627 with <S>/<E>) and ranks them easily
the grid costs a slot for every possible pair, which is fine at 27×27 and explodes when the context grows (the MLP course)

compare.q: This card reads a row of counts; the sampling card reads a row of probabilities. What changes when you divide by the row total, and what stays the same?
answer: the ranking within a row stays the same (e. is still first in the 'e' row)
rows become comparable because each sums to 1
zeros stay zero, so sampling can never produce an unseen pair

predict.q: The smoothing card adds 1 to every cell before normalising. After that, how many cells of N are zero, and what probability does the model now give to an empty name ('.' right after '.')?
predict.answer: No cells are zero any more. N[0,0] becomes 1 and row 0 totals 32,033 + 27 = 32,060, so an empty name gets probability 1/32,060 ≈ 0.0000312: tiny, but no longer impossible. The same fix is what keeps the loss finite for pairs the data never showed.

apply.task: Using your N, find the row with the most zero cells: count zeros per row with (N == 0).sum(1), print the winning row's nonzero cells and its total, and explain from those numbers why it is so sparse.
apply.done: You find the 'q' row with 16 zeros out of 27, a row total of 272, and qu = 206, so one pair takes 206 / 272 ≈ 75.7% of the row.
apply.hint: z = (N == 0).sum(1), then itos[z.argmax().item()]. The 'v' row comes second with 12 zeros.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the most common pair, or the number of zero cells?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why rows balance with columns, or why '.' pairs dominate?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: counting loop → row/column meaning, or zero cell → infinite loss later?
Could you rebuild the 28×28 version and predict its zero count (157) before running it?
What will you check first in your own N before moving on to sampling?
